---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:PierceThm}
Assume that $n \ge 6$ and ${\mathbb F}$ is an infinite field. If $T$ is a linear map on the space of all $n \times n$ matrices preserving the matrix discriminant, then $T$ has one of two forms:
$$
T(X) = cS^{-1}XS+\alpha(X)I_n\qquad\mbox{or}\qquad T(X) = cS^{-1}X^tS+\alpha(X)I_n
$$
where $S$ is an invertible matrix, $c^n = 1$, and $\alpha$ is a linear functional on the space of all $n\times n$ matrices, $X^t$ stands for the transpose of $X$, $I_n$ is the identity matrix.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:MainThmInIntro} Assume that $n \ge 3$ and $|{\mathbb F}| > n(n-1)$. Let $T$ be a linear map on the space of all $n\times n$ square matrices preserving the matrix discriminant. Then there are an invertible matrix $M$, a linear functional $\alpha$ on the space of all $n\times n$ matrices and $c \in {\mathbb F}$ such that $c^{n(n-1)} = 1$ and
\begin{equation}\notag                               
T(X) = cM^{-1}XM + \alpha(X)I_n\;\;\mbox{for every $n\times n$ matrix $X$}
\end{equation}
or
\begin{equation}\notag                               
T(X) = cM^{-1}X^tM + \alpha(X)I_n\;\;\mbox{for every $n\times n$ matrix $X$}.\footnote{The reader may notice that in contrast to the requirement $c^{n} = 1$ in the formulation of Theorem~\ref{thm:PierceThm} we require only that $c^{n(n-1)} = 1$. Indeed, from the property~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyH} of the matrix discriminant presented below we obtain that the linear map $X \mapsto cX$ preserves the matrix discriminant for all $c \in {\mathbb F}$ with $c^{n(n-1)} = 1$.}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
For a given $A \in {\mathcal M}_{m}({\mathbb F})$ ,we denote by $p_A(x) \in {\mathbb F}[x]$  its \emph{characteristic polynomial}, i.e.
\[
p_A(x) = \det(xI_m - A).
\]
We will use formula 
\begin{equation}\label{eqqq:formulaChPoly}
p_A(x) = x^m - E_1(A)x^{m-1} + E_2(A)x^{m-2} + \ldots + (-1)^m E_{m}(A),
\end{equation}
where $E_k(A)$ denotes the sum of all maximal minors of $A$. This formula could be found, e.g., in~\cite{Horn_Johnson_1985}.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $f,g \in {\mathbb F}[x]$ be polynomials and
\[f(x) = a_0 + \ldots + a_m x^m,\qquad g(x) = b_0 + \ldots + b_k x^k,\]
where $m + k \ge 1$, but $a_m$ or $b_k$ may be equal to zero. Then by\linebreak $\operatorname{Res}_{m\, k} (f,g) = \operatorname{Res}_{m\, k}(a_0,\ldots, a_m; b_0, \ldots, b_k)$ we denote the \emph{resultant} of $f$ and $g$ which is defined by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:DefRes}
\operatorname{Res}_{m\, k} (f,g) =
\begin{vmatrix}
a_m &  \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & a_1 & a_{0} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & 0\\
\vdots & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\ddots} & \vdots & \vdots & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\ddots} & \vdots\\
0 & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & a_m & a_{m-1} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & a_0\\
b_{k} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & b_1 & b_0 & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & 0 \\

\vdots & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\ddots} & \vdots & \vdots & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\ddots} & \vdots\\
0 & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & b_k & b_{k-1} & \multicolumn{1}{c}{\cdots} & b_{0}
\end{vmatrix}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The order of the determinant in the equality~(\ref{eq:DefRes}) is equal to $m + n.$
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:ResMultOneByScal}If $m + k \ge 1$, $f(x) = a_0 + \ldots + a_m x^m$ and $g(x) = b_0 + \ldots + b_k x^k$, then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:ResMultOneByScal:eqq1}
\operatorname{Res}_{m\, k}(\lambda f, \mu g) = \lambda^k \mu^m \operatorname{Res}_{m\, k}(f, g).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:ResReverse}If $m + k \ge 1$, $f(x) = a_0 + \ldots + a_m x^m$, $g(x) = b_0 + \ldots + b_k x^k$ and $f' = a_m + \ldots + a_0x^m$, $g' = b_k + \ldots + b_0x^k$, then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:ResReverse:eqq1}
\operatorname{Res}_{m\, k}(f',g') = (-1)^{mk}\operatorname{Res}_{m\, k}(f,g).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:ResXX0G}If $f(x) = x - x_0$, $g \in {\mathbb F}^{\le k}$, then 
\begin{equation}\label{cor:ResXX0G:eqq1}
\operatorname{Res}_{1\, k}(f,g) = g(x_0).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:ResSplitPoly}
\begin{equation}\label{cor:ResSplitPoly:eqq1}
\operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}\left(\prod_{i = 1}^{k} (x - x_i), g \right) = \prod_{i= 1}^m g(x_i)\quad\mbox{for all}\;\; x_1,  \ldots, x_m \in {\mathbb F}, g \in {\mathbb F}^{\le k}[x].
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:ResCommonRoot}
If $m + k \ge 1$ and $f \in {\mathbb F}^{\le m}[x], g \in {\mathbb F}^{\le k}[x] $ have a common root in ${\mathbb F}$, then $\operatorname{Res}_{m\,k} (f,g) = 0$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:ResReverseGradHomogen}If $f = a_0 + \ldots + a_mx^m, g = b_0 + \ldots + b_kx^k, \lambda \in {\mathbb F}[x],$ then \begin{equation}\label{lem:ResReverseGradHomogen:eqq1}
\operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}(\lambda^m a_0, \ldots, \lambda^0 a_m; \lambda^k b_0, \ldots, \lambda^0 b_k) = \lambda^{mk} \operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}(a_0, \ldots, a_m; b_0, \ldots, b_k).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Indeed,
\begin{multline*}
\operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}(\lambda^m a_0, \ldots, \lambda^0 a_m; \lambda^k b_0, \ldots, \lambda^0 b_k)\\
\overset{\eqref{lem:ResReverse:eqq1}}{=\joinrel=} (-1)^{mk} \operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}(\lambda^0 a_m, \ldots, \lambda^m a_0; \lambda^0 b_k, \ldots, \lambda^0 b_0)\\
\overset{\eqref{enum:ResWeightedMulLin}}{=\joinrel=} (-1)^{mk}\cdot \lambda^{mk} \operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}(a_m, \ldots, a_0; b_k, \ldots,  b_0)\\
\overset{\eqref{lem:ResReverse:eqq1}}{=\joinrel=}  (-1)^{mk}\cdot \lambda^{mk} \cdot (-1)^{mk} \operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}(a_0, \ldots, a_m; b_0, \ldots, b_k)\\
 = \lambda^{mk}\operatorname{Res}_{m\,k}(a_0, \ldots, a_m; b_0, \ldots, b_k).
\end{multline*}
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:PolyDiscriminant}Let $m \ge 1$ be integer and let $f \in {\mathbb F}[x]$ be a polynomial with 
\begin{equation}\label{def:PolyDiscriminant:eq1}
f(x) = a_0 + \ldots + a_m x^m,\quad a_0, \ldots, a_m \in {\mathbb F}
\end{equation}
We denote by\linebreak $\operatorname{D}_{m}(f) = \operatorname{D}(a_0,\ldots, a_m)$  \emph{a discriminant} of $f,$ which is defined by
\[
\operatorname{D}_m(f)  = \frac{(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}}{a_m} \operatorname{Res}_{m\,(m-1)}(f, f'),
\]
where $f'$ is a formal derivative $f$. In addition, if $f$ in~\eqref{def:PolyDiscriminant:eq1} is monic, then we allow to omit the subscript and use the notion $\operatorname{D}(f)$ instead of $\operatorname{D}_m(f)$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:DPolyN2}
Let $f =  x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DPolyN2:eqq1}
\operatorname{D}(f) = 4a_0 - a_1^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:D2PolyN2Char2}
Assume that $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. If $f = x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$, then $\operatorname{D}(f) = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}^2(f)$ for $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f)$ defined by
\begin{equation}\label{lem:D2PolyN2Char2:eqq1}
\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f) = a_1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:DPolyN3}
Let $f = x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DPolyN3:eqq1}
\operatorname{D}(f) = -27a_0^2 - 4a_1^3 + 18a_0a_1a_2 + a_1^2a_2^2 - 4a_0^2a_2^3.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:D2PolyN3Char2}
Assume that $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. If $f = x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$, then $\operatorname{D}(f) = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}^2(f)$ for $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f)$ defined by
\begin{equation}\label{lem:D2PolyN3Char2:eqq1}
\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f) = a_0 + a_1a_2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:DPolyN3Char3}
Assume that $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 3$. Let $f = x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DPolyN3Char3:eqq1}
\operatorname{D}(f) = 2a_1^3 + a_0^2a_1^2 + 2a_0^2a_2^3.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:DiscN4FormulaCHN2}Let $f = x^4 + a_3 x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$. Then 
\begin{multline}\label{lem:DiscN4FormulaCHN2:eqq1}
\operatorname{D}(f) = 256 a_0^3 - 27 a_1^4 + 144 a_0 a_1^2 a_2 - 128 a_0^2 a_2^2 - 4 a_1^2 a_2^3 + 16 a_0 a_2^4\\
 - 192 a_0^2 a_1 a_3 + 18 a_1^3 a_2 a_3 - 80 a_0 a_1 a_2^2 a_3 - 6 a_0 a_1^2 a_3^2 + 144 a_0^2 a_2 a_3^2\\
  + a_1^2 a_2^2 a_3^2 - 4 a_0 a_2^3 a_3^2 - 4 a_1^3 a_3^3 + 18 a_0 a_1 a_2 a_3^3 - 27 a_0^2 a_3^4.
\end{multline}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:Disc2N4FormulaCH2}Assume that $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. If $f = x^4 + a_3 x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$, then $\operatorname{D}(f) = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}^2(f)$ for $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f)$ defined by 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:Disc2N4FormulaCH2:eqq1}
\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f) = a_1^2  + a_1 a_2 a_3 + a_0 a_3^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:Disc2N5FormulaCH2}
Assume that $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. If $f = x^5 + a_4x^4 + a_3 x^3 + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0$, then $\operatorname{D}(f) = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}^2(f)$ for $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f)$ defined by 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:Disc2N5FormulaCH2:eqq1}
\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(f) = a_0^2 + a_1 a_2^2 + a_0 a_2 a_3 + a_1 a_2 a_3 a_4 + a_0 a_3^2 a_4 + a_1^2 a_4^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:D2ExistsAndUniqueN2to5}Assume that $1 \le n \le 5$ and $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. Then there exists a unique polynomial $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}} \in {\mathbb F}[a_{0}, \ldots, a_{n-1}]$ such that $\operatorname{D}(f) = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}^2(f)$ for all monic $f \in {\mathbb F}^{\le n}[x]$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The existence of such a polynomial follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:D2PolyN2Char2}, Corollary~\ref{cor:D2PolyN3Char2}, Corollary~\ref{cor:Disc2N4FormulaCH2}, Corollary~\ref{cor:Disc2N5FormulaCH2} and from the definition of the discriminant for $n =1$. The uniqueness follows from the fact that if $\left(P_1\right)^2 = \left(P_2\right)^2$ for some $P_1, P_2 \in  {\mathbb F}[a_{0}, \ldots, a_{n-1}]$, then $(P_1 - P_2)^2 = 0$ and consequently $P_1 - P_2 = 0$ because the ring  ${\mathbb F}[a_{0}, \ldots, a_{n-1}]$ is a domain.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The statement of Lemma~\ref{lem:D2ExistsAndUniqueN2to5} is true for all $n$, but we do not need to establish it in the full generality in this paper.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
Assume that $1 \le n \le 5$  and $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. We define a polynomial $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}} \in {\mathbb F}[a_{0}, \ldots, a_{n-1}]$ which is defined for the monic polynomials belonging to ${\mathbb F}^{\le n}[x]$ as it is done in Corollary~\ref{cor:D2PolyN2Char2}, Corollary~\ref{cor:D2PolyN3Char2}, Corollary~\ref{cor:Disc2N4FormulaCH2}  and Corollary~\ref{cor:Disc2N5FormulaCH2}. For $n = 1$ we define $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}$ by $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}} = 1$.

Lemma~\ref{lem:D2ExistsAndUniqueN2to5} implies that $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}$ is uniquely determined by the equality $\operatorname{D} = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}^2$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
If $X \in {\mathcal M}_{m}({\mathbb F})$, then by $\operatorname{D} (X)$ we denote a discriminant of the characteristic polynomial of $X.$ It is called  \emph{a discriminant} of $X.$ In other words,
\[
\operatorname{D}(X) = \operatorname{D}(p_X(x)) = \operatorname{D} (\det (x I_m - X)).
\]
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The above formulas show how the matrix discriminant of a matrix $X$ is expressed as a resultant of its characteristic polynomial $p_X$ and the derivative of $p_X$. Apart from that, is also possible to express $\operatorname{D}(X)$ through the traces of powers of $X$  (see~\cite{Parlett2002}).
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:N3CharPoly}Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_{2}({\mathbb F})$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D2Formula}
\operatorname{D}(A) = 4\det(A) - \operatorname{tr}(A)^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Indeed, if $A \in {\mathcal M}_{2}({\mathbb F})$, then $p_A(x) = x^2 - \operatorname{tr}(A)x + \det(A)$ by the formula~\eqref{eqqq:formulaChPoly}. Then, by applying Lemma~\ref{lem:DPolyN2} to $p_A$, we obtain~\eqref{eq:D2Formula}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:DiscDirSum}Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_{(n + m)}({\mathbb F}), A_0 \in {\mathcal M}_n({\mathbb F})$ and $A' \in {\mathcal M}_{m}({\mathbb F})$ be such that $A'$ is strictly upper triangular and
\[
A = \left[\begin{array}{ c | c }
    A_0 & * \\
    \hline
    0 & A'
  \end{array}\right],
\]
where $*$ is an $n\times m$ matrix. Then for every $B_0 \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ and $b_1,\ldots, b_m \in {\mathbb F}$ 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DiscDirSum:eqq1}
\operatorname{D}\left(A + B\right) = \operatorname{D}(A_0 + B_0)  \prod_{1 \le k \le m} p_{(A_0 + B_0)}^2 (b_k) \prod_{1 \le i < j \le m} (b_i - b_j)^2,
\end{equation}
where $B = \left(B_0 \oplus \operatorname{diag}(b_1, \ldots, b_k)\right).$
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Indeed, since $A'$ is strictly upper triangular and $*$ does not affect on $p_{(A+B)}$, then
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DiscDirSum:eq1}
p_{(A+B)} = p_{(A_0 + B_0)} \oplus \operatorname{diag}(b_1, \ldots, b_m)
\end{equation}
and consequently
\begin{multline*}
\operatorname{D}\left(A + B\right) = \operatorname{D}(p_{(A + B)})
\overset{\eqref{lem:DiscDirSum:eq1}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=}\operatorname{D} \left(p_{(A_0 + B_0)} \oplus p_{\operatorname{diag}(b_1,\ldots, b_m)}\right)\\
 \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Property~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyProd}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \operatorname{D}(A_0 + B_0) \operatorname{Res}_{n\,m}^2(p_{(A_0 + B_0)}, p_{\operatorname{diag}(b_1,\ldots, b_m)}) D(\operatorname{diag}(b_1,\ldots, b_m))\\
= \operatorname{D}(A_0 + B_0) \operatorname{Res}_{n\,m}^2(p_{(A_0 + B_0)}, \prod_{1 \le k \le m} (x - b_k) D(\operatorname{diag}(b_1,\ldots, b_m)\\
\overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Property~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyDiag}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \operatorname{D}(A_0 + B_0) \operatorname{Res}_{n\,m}^2(p_{(A' + B_0)}, \prod_{1 \le k \le m} (x - b_k) \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (b_i - b_j)^2\\
\overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Property~\ref{enum:ResProduct}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \operatorname{D}(A_0 + B_0)   \prod_{1 \le k \le n} p_{(A_0 + B_0)}^2 (b_k) \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (b_i - b_j)^2.
\end{multline*}
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Assume that $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$ and $1 \le m \le 5$. If $X \in {\mathcal M}_{m}({\mathbb F})$, then $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(X)$ is defined by
\[
\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(X) = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(p_X(x)) = \operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}(\det (x I_m - X)).
\]
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:PresDEqPresD2}
Assume that $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. Let $T\colon {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F}) \to {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be a linear map. Then $T$ preserves $\operatorname{D}$ if and only if $T$ preserves $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Indeed, if $\operatorname{char} ({\mathbb F}) = 2$, then the conditions $a^2 = b^2$ are $a = b$ equivalent for $a, b \in {\mathbb F}$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:radical}Let ${\mathbb F}$ be a field, $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over ${\mathbb F}$, and let $f$ be a function from $V$ to ${\mathbb F}$. The \emph{radical} of $f$, denoted by $\operatorname{rad} (f)$ is a subset of $V$ defined by
\[
\operatorname{rad} (f) = \{\mathbf w \mid f(\mathbf v + \lambda \mathbf w) = f(\mathbf v)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; \mathbf v \in V,\;\; \lambda \in {\mathbb F}\}.
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:KernelContainedInRad}If $T\colon V \to V$ is a linear map preserving $f$, then $\operatorname{ker} T \subseteq \operatorname{rad}(f)$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Indeed, assume that $\mathbf w \in \operatorname{ker} T.$ Then
\begin{equation*}
f(\mathbf v + \lambda\mathbf w)= f(T(\mathbf v + \lambda\mathbf w))\\
= f(T(\mathbf v) + \lambda T(\mathbf w)) = f(T(\mathbf v) + \mathbf 0) = f(\mathbf v)
\end{equation*}
for all $\mathbf v \in V$ and $\lambda \in {\mathbb F}$. Therefore, $\mathbf w \in \operatorname{rad}(f)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The lemma above is implicitly proved in~\cite{Waterhouse1983} (see~\cite[Proposition~1]{Waterhouse1983}).
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:RadicalInvariant}
Let $V$ be a vector space over ${\mathbb F}$, $f\colon V \to {\mathbb F}$ be an arbitrary function. If $f$ has trivial radical, then the set of all linear maps preserving $f$ form a group. If $f$ has nontrivial radical $\operatorname{rad}(f)$, let $\pi_{rad}\colon V \to V/\operatorname{rad}(f)$ be the projection, and write $f = f_{\operatorname{rad}} \circ \pi_{\operatorname{rad}}$. Then the linear map $T \colon V \to V$ preserves $f$ if and only if
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=(\alph*)]
\item\label{lem:RadicalInvariant:part1} $T(\operatorname{rad}(f)) \subseteq \operatorname{rad}(f)$  and
\item\label{lem:RadicalInvariant:part2} the map $T_{\operatorname{rad}} \colon V / \operatorname{rad}(f) \to V / \operatorname{rad}(f)$ that is given by $T_{\operatorname{rad}}(\pi_{\operatorname{rad}}(\mathbf v)) = \pi_{\operatorname{rad}}(T(\mathbf v))$ (and is well defined because of~\ref{lem:RadicalInvariant:part1}) preserves $f_{\operatorname{rad}}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
Let ${\mathbb F}$ be an infinite field. Let $f$ be a
polynomial in $n$ variables over ${\mathbb F}$. If $f$ defines the zero function on ${\mathbb F}^{n}$, then $f = 0$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
Let ${\mathbb F}$ be a finite field with $q$ elements. Let $f$ be a
polynomial in $n$ variables over ${\mathbb F}$ such that the degree of $f$ in each variable
is less than $q$. If $f$ defines the zero function on ${\mathbb F}^{n}$, then $f = 0$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{DegFLessZero}Let ${\mathbb F}$ be an arbitrary field. Let $f$ be a
polynomial in $n$ variables over ${\mathbb F}$ such that either ${\mathbb F}$ is infinite or the degree of $f$ in each variable
is less than $|{\mathbb F}|$. If $f$ defines the zero function on ${\mathbb F}^{n}$, then $f = 0$.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{DegFGLessEqual}Let $f, g$ be a
polynomials in $n$ variables over ${\mathbb F}$ such that either ${\mathbb F}$ is infinite or the degree of $f$ and $g$ in each variable
is less than $|{\mathbb F}|$. If $f$ and $g$ define the same function on ${\mathbb F}^{n}$, then $f = g$.
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:ManyPolyDensityArg}
Let $\mathcal S \subseteq {\mathbb F}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ and $0 \neq Q \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$  be such that $\deg(P) + \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$ for all $P \in \mathcal S$. If 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:ManyPolyDensityArg:eqq1}
\left(Q(\mathbf x) \neq 0\right) \Rightarrow \left(\forall P \in \mathcal S\colon P(\mathbf x) = 0 \right)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n,
\end{equation}
  then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:ManyPolyDensityArg:eqq2}
P(\mathbf x) = 0\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n, P \in \mathcal S\;\;\mbox{(i.e., $\mathcal S = \{0\}$)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Indeed, if $0 \neq P \in \mathcal S$, then $PQ \neq 0$ and $\deg(PQ) = \deg(P) + \deg(Q) \le |{\mathbb F}|$ by the assumptions of the lemma. Hence, there is $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n$ such that $PQ(\mathbf x) \neq 0$ by Corollary~\ref{DegFLessZero}. This implies that $Q(\mathbf x) \neq 0$ and $P(\mathbf x) \neq 0$, which contradicts~\eqref{lem:ManyPolyDensityArg:eqq1}. Therefore, the equality~\eqref{lem:ManyPolyDensityArg:eqq2} holds for all $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n, P \in \mathcal S.$
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:JabMat}
Given $\mathbf a, \mathbf b \in {\mathbb F}^n,$ we denote
\[
J(\mathbf a, \mathbf b) = \begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf a_1\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf b_1\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf b_n\\
\end{pmatrix} & \cdots & \mathbf a_n\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf b_1\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf b_n\\
\end{pmatrix}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
i.e., $(J(\mathbf a,\mathbf b))_{i\,j} = \mathbf b_i \mathbf a_j,$ $1 \le i, j \le n.$
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
It is possible to use the language of tensor algebra  to discuss about the matrices of rank 1 as it done in certain papers (e.g. in~\cite{Botta1983}). However, it requires the explicit specification of correspondence between tensors and matrices.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp} If $C \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ is such that $\operatorname{rk}(C) = 1$ and $c_{i\,i} = c_{j\,j} \neq 0$ for all $1 \le i, j \le n$, then there are $0\neq c, c_1, \ldots, c_n \in {\mathbb F}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eqq1}
c_{i\,j} = c c_{i} c^{-1}_{j}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i, j \le n.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $c \in F$ be the common value of the entries belonging to the main diagonal of $C$, i.e., $c$ is such that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq2}
c = c_{i\,i} \neq 0\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i \le n.
\end{equation}
Since $\operatorname{rk}(C) = 1$, then $\operatorname{\mathbf C}(C) = \langle\mathbf v\rangle$ for some $0 \neq \mathbf v \in {\mathbb F}^n$. Hence, there is $0 \neq \mathbf a \in {\mathbb F}^n$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq1}
C = J(\mathbf a,\mathbf v).
\end{equation}
The equality~\eqref{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq1} implies in particular that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq3}
\mathbf a_{i}\mathbf v_{i} = c_{i\,i} \overset{\eqref{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq2}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} c\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i \le n.
\end{equation}
Thus, since $c \neq 0$, then $\mathbf a_{i}, \mathbf v_{i} \neq 0$ for all $1 \le i \le n$. This allows to rewrite~\eqref{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq3} as follows
\begin{equation}\label{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq4}
\mathbf a_{i} =  c \mathbf v^{-1}_{i}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i \le n.
\end{equation}
Now, by setting 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq5}
c_i = \mathbf v_{i}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i \le n
\end{equation}
we obtain that $c$ and $c_1, \ldots, c_n$ satisfy the condition~\eqref{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eqq1}. Indeed,
\begin{multline*}
c_{i\,j} = \left(J(\mathbf a,\mathbf v)\right)_{i\,j} \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Definition~\ref{def:JabMat}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \mathbf a_{j} \mathbf v_{i} = \mathbf v_{i} \mathbf a_{j}\\
\overset{\eqref{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq4}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=}  \mathbf v_{i} \left(c \mathbf v^{-1}_{j}\right) \overset{\eqref{lem:MatRkOneConstDiagDecomp:eq5}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} c  c_{i} c_{j}^{-1}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i, j \le n.
\end{multline*}
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:RK1Sim} Let ${\mathbb F}$ be an arbitrary field and $J \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be a rank-one matrix. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=(\alph*)]
\item $J$ is nilpotent if and only if $J$ is similar to $E_{1\,2}$.
\item $J$ is non-nilpotent if and only if $J$ is similar to $cE_{1\,1}$ for some $0 \neq c \in {\mathbb F}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
It is clear that if $J$ is similar to $E_{1\,2}$, then it is nilpotent, and if $J$ is similar to $cE_{1\,1}$ for some $0 \neq c \in {\mathbb F}$, then $J$ is non-nilpotent. Thus, it is suffices to show the following:
\begin{enumerate}[label=Claim~(\roman*), ref=(\roman*), leftmargin=*]
\item\label{lem:RK1Sim:claim1} If $J$ is nilpotent, then $J$ is similar to $E_{1\,2}$.
\item\label{lem:RK1Sim:claim2} If $J$ is non-nilpotent, then $J$ is similar to $cE_{1\,1}$ for some $0 \neq c \in {\mathbb F}$.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Proof of Claim~\ref{lem:RK1Sim:claim1}} Let $0 \neq \mathbf v$ be such that $\operatorname{\mathbf C} (J) = \langle v \rangle$.  Since $J$ is nilpotent, then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RK1Sim:eq12}
J\mathbf v = \mathbf 0
\end{equation}
and consequently $\mathbf v \in \ker J$. Let $\mathbf v'$ be such that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RK1Sim:eq11}
J\mathbf v' = \mathbf v.
\end{equation}

By rank-nullity theorem, $\dim(\ker J) = n - 1$. Let us extend $\mathbf v$ to a basis $\mathbf v^{(1)} = \mathbf v, \mathbf v^{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf v^{(n-1)}$ of $\ker J$. The equality~\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq11} implies that the vectors $\mathbf v', \mathbf v^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf v^{(n-1)}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, these vectors form a basis of ${\mathbb F}^n$. 

Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be a matrix such that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RK1Sim:eq1}
A\mathbf e^{(1)} = \mathbf v^{(1)},\; A\mathbf e^{(2)} = \mathbf v',\;\mbox{and}\; A\mathbf e^{(i)} = A\mathbf v^{(i-2)}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;3 \le i \le n.
\end{equation}
Since $\mathbf v', \mathbf v^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf v^{(n-1)}$ form a basis of ${\mathbb F}^n$, then $A$ is invertible. Let $J' = A^{-1}JA$. Then
\begin{equation*}
J'\mathbf e^{(1)} = A^{-1}JA\mathbf e^{(1)} \overset{\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq1}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} A^{-1}J\mathbf v \overset{\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq12}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \mathbf 0,
\end{equation*}
\begin{equation*}
J'\mathbf e^{(2)} = A^{-1}JA\mathbf e^{(2)} \overset{\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq1}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} A^{-1}J\mathbf v' \overset{\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq11}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} A^{-1}\mathbf v \overset{\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq1}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \mathbf e^{(1)},
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
J'\mathbf e^{(i)} = A^{-1}JA\mathbf e^{(i)} \overset{\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq1}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} A^{-1}J\mathbf v^{(i-2)} \overset{\mathbf v^{(i-2)} \in \ker J}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \mathbf 0\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;3 \le i \le n.
\end{equation*}
Therefore, $J' = E_{1\,2}$  and Claim~\ref{lem:RK1Sim:claim1} is established.
 
\paragraph{Proof of Claim~\ref{lem:RK1Sim:claim2}} Let $0 \neq \mathbf v$ be such that $\operatorname{\mathbf C} (J) = \langle v \rangle$.  Since $J$ is non-nilpotent, then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RK1Sim:eq13}
J\mathbf v = c \mathbf v\;\;\mbox{for some}\;\;0 \neq c \in {\mathbb F}.
\end{equation}
By rank-nullity theorem, $\dim(\ker J) = n - 1$. Let $\mathbf u^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf u^{(n-1)}$ be a basis of $\ker J$. The equality~\eqref{lem:RK1Sim:eq13} implies that $\mathbf v, \mathbf u^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf u^{(n-1)}$ are linearly independent. Therefore, these vectors form a basis of ${\mathbb F}^n$. 

Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be a matrix such that 
\begin{equation}\notag
A\mathbf e^{(1)} = \mathbf v^{(1)},\;\mbox{and}\;  A\mathbf e^{(i)} = A\mathbf u^{(i-1)}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;2 \le i \le n.
\end{equation}
Since $\mathbf v, \mathbf u^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf u^{(n-1)}$ form a basis of ${\mathbb F}^n$, then $A$ is invertible. Let $J' = A^{-1}JA$. By the same calculations as for the previous case we obtain that $J' = cE_{1\,1}$ which establishes Claim~\ref{lem:RK1Sim:claim2}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:Rset}By ${\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}) \subseteq {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ we denote the set of all matrices of the form $J + cI_n$, where $\operatorname{rk}(J) \le 1$ and $c \in {\mathbb F}$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:RsetProp}If $M \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ is an invertible matrix and $c \in {\mathbb F}$, then\linebreak $M{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})M^{-1} + cI_n = {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
It is clear that ${\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}) + cI_n = {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})$. Hence, it is sufficient to show only that $M{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})M^{-1} = {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F})$. 
Let $X \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})$. By the definition, there are $J \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ and $c \in {\mathbb F}$ such that $\operatorname{rk}(J) \le 1$ and $X = J + cI_n$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RsetProp:eq1}
MXM^{-1} = MJM^{-1} + cI_n.
\end{equation}
The similarity transformation preserves the rank of a matrix 
(see, for example~\cite[Theorem 3.4]{Friedberg2002-wu}). Therefore, the equality~\eqref{lem:RsetProp:eq1} implies that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RsetProp:eq2}
MXM \in {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F}).
\end{equation}
The inclusion~\eqref{lem:RsetProp:eq2} holds for all $X \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})$. This establishes the inclusion $M{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})M^{-1} \subseteq {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F})$. In order to prove that $M{\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})M^{-1} = {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ we need to establish the reverse inclusion, which is obtained similarly.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField}Assume that ${\mathbb F}' \supseteq {\mathbb F}$ are fields and $n \ge 3$. Let $B \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$. If $B \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}'),$ then $B \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}).$
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let  $B \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$, $c' \in {\mathbb F}'$ and $J'\in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F}')$ be such that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField:eqq1}
B =  J' + c'I_n
\end{equation}
and $\operatorname{rk}(J') \le 1$. If $\operatorname{rk}(J')=0$, then $J' = O_n$. Hence, the equality~\eqref{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField:eqq1} and the condition $B \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ imply that $c' \in {\mathbb F}$. Therefore, $J \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ and $c' \in {\mathbb F}$ which implies that $B \in {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F})$.

Assume now that $\operatorname{rk}(J') = 1$. Note that this equality~\eqref{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField:eqq1} implies that all entries of $J'$ not lying on its main diagonal belong to ${\mathbb F}$. There are two cases possible:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item All entries of $J'$ not lying on the main diagonal are equal to zero.
  \item There are $1 \le i \neq j \le n$ such that $J'_{i\,j} \neq 0$.
\end{enumerate}
We consider them separately.

\paragraph{All entries of $J'$ not lying on the main diagonal are equal to zero} Since $\operatorname{rk}\left(J'\right) = 1$, then this assumption implies that there is only one non-zero element in $J'$ lying on the main diagonal. Since $n \ge 3$, from this and~\eqref{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField:eqq1} we conclude that $c' \in {\mathbb F}$. Therefore, $J' \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$. Thus, all the summands in the right-hand side of~\eqref{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField:eqq1} belong to ${\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ consequently  $B \in {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F})$.

\paragraph{There are $1 \le i \neq j \le n$ such that $J'_{i\,j} \neq 0$} Since $n \ge 3,$ there is $1 \le k \le n$ such that $i\,j \neq k$. Since $J'$ is a rank-one matrix, then every $2\times 2$ minor of $J'$ is equal to zero. In particular, $\det\left(J''[i, k| j, k]\right) = 0.$ By expressing it through elements of $J'',$ we obtain that
\[
J'_{i\,j}J'_{k\,k} - J'_{i\,k} J'_{k\,j} = 0.
\] 
Since $J'_{i\,k}$ and  $J'_{k\,j}$ are not lying on the main diagonal of $J''$, then they belong to ${\mathbb F}$. Hence, 
\[
J'_{i\,j}J'_{k\,k} \in {\mathbb F}
\]
Similarly to $J'_{i\,k}$ and  $J'_{k\,j}$, the multiplier $J'_{i\,j}$ belongs to ${\mathbb F}$ and is not equal to zero by the assumption made for this case. Hence, $J'_{k\,k} \in {\mathbb F}$. By considering the $(k,k)$-th elements in the summands of both the sides of the equality~\eqref{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField:eqq1}, we obtain that
\[
b_{k\,k} = c' + J'_{k\,k} \in {\mathbb F}.
\]
Therefore, $c' \in {\mathbb F}$, which implies that $J' \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$. This means that all the summands in the right-hand side of~\eqref{lem:RankOneScalarFromExtToGroundField:eqq1} belong to ${\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ which infers that $B \in {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F})$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:DiagonalR1Crit}Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be a diagonal matrix. Then $A \in {\mathfrak R}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq1}
\forall 1 \le i_1 < i_2 < i_3 \le n\;\; \exists 1 \le \alpha < \beta \le 3  \colon a_{i_\alpha\,i_\alpha} = a_{i_\beta\,i_\beta} 
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq2}
\forall 1 \le i_1 < i_2 < i_3 < i_4 \le n\;\; \exists 1 \le \alpha < \beta < \gamma \le 4 \colon a_{i_\alpha\,i_\alpha} = a_{i_\beta\,i_\beta} = a_{i_\gamma\,i_\gamma}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Assume that $A \in {\mathfrak R}_{n}$. This implies that there is $c \in {\mathbb F}$ such that $\operatorname{rk}(A - cI_n) \le 1$. Hence, $A - cI_n$ has at most one nonzero entry and consequently satisfies the conditions~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq1} and~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq2}. These conditions are preserved by addition of a scalar matrix. Therefore, $A$ satisfies these conditions as well.

Assume now that $A$ is diagonal matrix such that the conditions~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq1} and~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq2} hold. The condition~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq1} implies that $|\{a_{i\,i} \mid 1 \le i \le n\}| \le 2$. If $|\{a_{i\,i} \mid 1 \le i \le n\}| = 1$, then $A - a_{1\,1} = O_n$ and the statement of the lemma is established. Consider now the case where $|\{a_{i\,i} \mid 1 \le i \le n\}| = 2$. 

Let $1 \le i_1 < i_2 \le n$ are such that $a_{i_1\,i_1} \neq a_{i_2\,i_2}$. The condition~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq2} implies that either $|\{i \mid a_{i\,i} = a_{i_1\,i_1}, 1 \le i \le n\}| = 1$, or $|\{i \mid a_{i\,i} = a_{i_2\,i_2}, 1 \le i \le n\}| = 1.$ Assume without loss of generality that $|\{i \mid a_{i\,i} = a_{i_1\,i_1}, 1 \le i \le n\}| = 1.$ Then $A - a_{i_2\,i_2}I_n$ is a diagonal matrix with only one nonzero entry. Therefore, $\operatorname{rk}(A - a_{i_2\,i_2}I_n) = 1$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn} Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_n({\mathbb F})$, $1 \le i_1 \neq i_2 \le n$, $1 \le j_1 \neq j_2 \le n$ and  $P \in {\mathbb F}[x; a_{1\,1}, \ldots, a_{n\,n}$ be defined by
\[
P = \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]\right),
\]
where  $A^{(x)} \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ is defined by $A^{(x)} = A - xI_n$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=(\alph*)]
\item\label{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn:prop1} $\deg_x(P) \le 2$.
\item\label{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn:prop2} If $\deg_x(P) = 2$, then ($i_1 = j_1$ and $i_2 = j_2$) or ($i_1 = j_2$ and $i_2 = j_1$). 
\item\label{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn:prop3} $[i]P$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2-i$ for all $0 \le i \le 2$.
 \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The properties~\eqref{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn:prop1} and~\eqref{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn:prop3} follow directly from the fact that the determinant of $2\times 2$ matrix is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 2 in the entries of a given matrix.

Assume now that $\deg_x(P) = 2$. This implies that the matrix
$A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]$ contains two diagonal elements of the matrix $A^{(x)}$. Therefore, $i_1 = j_1$ and $i_2 = j_2$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:RDetProp}Let $f, g, h \in {\mathbb F}^{\le 2}[x]$. Consider $R_{f\,g\,h} \in {\mathcal M}_{3}({\mathbb F})$ defined by
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RDetProp:eqq1}
R_{f\,g\,h} = \begin{pmatrix}[2]f & [1]f & [0]f\\ [2]g & [1]g & [0]g\\ [2]h & [1]h & [0]h\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation}
Then 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*), ref=(\alph*)]
\item\label{lem:RDetProp:prop1} if $c \in {\mathbb F}$,  $f' = f(x + c), g' = g(x + c), h' = h(x+c)$, then $\det\left(R_{f'\,g'\,h'}\right) = \det\left(R_{f\,g\,h}\right);$
\item\label{lem:RDetProp:prop2}  if there is $x_0 \in {\mathbb F}$ such that $f(x_0) = g(x_0) = h(x_0)$, then $\det\left(R_{f\,g\,h}\right) = 0$.
 \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The property~\ref{lem:RDetProp:prop1} of $R_{f\,g\,h}$ follows from the multilinearity of the determinant along the columns of the matrix $R_{f\,g\,h}$.

Now assume that $f(x_0) = g(x_0) = h(x_0)$ for some $x_0 \in {\mathbb F}$. This implies that the columns of the matrix $R_{f\, g\, h}$ are linearly dependent. Hence, $\det\left(R_{f\,g\,h}\right) = 0$. This establishes~\ref{lem:RDetProp:prop2}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit}Assume that $n \ge 3$. Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_n({\mathbb F})$ and $A^{(x)} \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F}[x])$ be defined by $A^{(x)} = A - xI_n$. Then $A \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1}
 \operatorname{Res}_{1\,2}\left(\det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,k|j_1,k]\right), \det\left(A^{(x)}[i'_1,i'_2|j'_1,j'_2]\right)\right) = 0
\end{equation}
 for all $1 \le i_1, j_1, k \le n,$ $1 \le i'_1 < i'_2 \le n,$ $1 \le j'_1 < j'_2 \le n$ such that $k \neq i_1, j_1$, $i_1 \neq j_1$,
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12}
 \operatorname{Res}_{2\,2}\left(\det\left(A^{(x)}[k_1,k_2|k_1,k_2]\right), \det\left(A^{(x)}[k_3,k_4|k_3,k_4]\right)\right) = 0
\end{equation}
 for all pairwise distinct $1 \le k_1, k_2, k_3, k_4 \le n$
and
 \begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2}
 \begin{vmatrix}
 [2]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right) & [1]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right) & [0]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right)\\
  [2]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right) & [1]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,k|i,k]\right) & [0]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,k|i,k]\right)\\
  [2]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right) & [1]\det \left(A^{(x)}[j,k|j,k]\right) & [0]\det \left(A^{(x)}[j,k|j,k]\right)
 \end{vmatrix} = 0
\end{equation}
for all $1 \le i < j < k \le n$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
First note that Lemma~\ref{lem:RDetProp} implies that the resultants in~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1}\linebreak and~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12} are defined correctly.

Let us prove the necessity. Assume that $A \in {\mathfrak R}_{n}$. This implies that there is $c \in {\mathbb F}$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq1}
\operatorname{rk}(A') \le 1,
\end{equation}
 where $A' = A - cI_n$. The condition~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq1} implies that every $2\times 2$ minor of $A'$ is zero and consequently all polynomials of the form $\det\left(\left(A'\right)^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]\right)$ for $1 \le i_1 < i_2 \le n,$ $1 \le  j_1 < j_2 \le n$  have the common root $x = 0$. Therefore, $A'$ satisfies the conditions~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1}, \eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12} by Corollary~\ref{cor:ResCommonRoot} and the condition~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2} by Lemma~\ref{lem:RDetProp}\ref{lem:RDetProp:prop2}.
 
 

 
The conditions~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1} and~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12} are preserved by addition of a scalar matrix by the properties~\ref{enum:ResPropertyC} and~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyC}, while the condition~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2} is preserved by this operation by Lemma~\ref{lem:RDetProp}\ref{lem:RDetProp:prop1}. Therefore, $A = A' + cI_n$ satisfies these conditions as well.

Let us prove the sufficiency of the conditions~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1}  and~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2} by contradiction. Suppose that $A \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ satisfies these conditions and 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq2}
A \not\in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}).
\end{equation}
 Let us consider the following two cases separately
\begin{enumerate}[label=Case (\alph*), ref=(\alph*), leftmargin = *]
\item\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:case1} $A$ is non-diagonal
\item\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:case2} $A$ is diagonal
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Case~\ref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:case1}}  Let $1 \le i_0 < j_0 \le n$ be such that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq10002}
a_{i_0\,j_0} \neq 0.
\end{equation}
Since $n \ge 3,$ then there is $1 \le k_0 \le n$ such that $k_0 \neq i_0, j_0$. Let $P(x) \in {\mathbb F}[x]$ be defined by
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq2222}
P = \det(A^{(x)}[i_0, k_0| j_0, k_0]) =   
a_{i_0\,k_0}a_{k_0\,j_0} - a_{i_0\,j_0}(a_{k_0\,k_0} - x)
\end{equation}
Since $a_{i_0\,j_0} \neq 0,$ there is $c_0 \in {\mathbb F}$ such that $P(c_0) = 0$. From~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq2222} we obtain that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq10003}
c_0 = a_{k_0\,k_0} - \frac{a_{i_0\,k_0}a_{k_0\,j_0}}{a_{i_0\,j_0}}.
\end{equation}
From the assumption that $A \not\in R_{n}({\mathbb F})$ we conclude that $\operatorname{rk}(A - c_0I_n) \ge 2$ and consequently there are $1 \le i_1 < i_2 \le n$ and $1 \le j_1 < j_2 \le 2$ such that 

\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq10004}
\det((A - c_0I_n)[i_1, i_2| j_1, j_2]) \neq 0.
\end{equation}
Therefore,
\begin{multline*}
\operatorname{Res}_{1\,2}\left(\det\left(A^{(x)}[i_0,k_0|j_0,k_0]\right), \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]\right)\right) = \\
\overset{\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq2222}}{=\joinrel=} \operatorname{Res}_{1\,2}\left(a_{i_0\,k_0}a_{k_0\,j_0} - a_{i_0\,j_0}(a_{k_0\,k_0} - x), \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]\right)\right)\phantom{X}\\
\phantom{XX}\overset{\eqref{lem:ResMultOneByScal:eqq1}}{=\joinrel=} a_{i_0\,j_0}^2 \operatorname{Res}_{1\,2}\left(x + \frac{a_{i_0\,k_0}a_{k_0\,j_0}}{a_{i_0\,j_0}} - a_{k_0\,k_0}, \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]\right)\right)\\
\overset{\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq10003}}{=\joinrel=} a_{i_0\,j_0}^2 \operatorname{Res}_{1\,2}\left(x - c_0, \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]\right)\right)\\
\overset{\eqref{cor:ResXX0G:eqq1}}{=\joinrel=}  a_{i_0\,j_0}^2  \det((A - c_0I_n)[i_1, i_2| j_1, j_2]) \overset{\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq10002},\, \eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq10004}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel\neq\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} 0,
\end{multline*} 
 which contradicts~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1}.

\paragraph{Case~\ref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:case2}} Since $A$ is diagonal, then the condition~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq2} and Lemma~\ref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit} imply that $A$ violates at least one of the conditions~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq1} or~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq2}. Let us consider these subcases separately.

\subparagraph{$A$ does not satisfy the condition~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq1}} If $1 \le i  < j < k \le n$ are such that the condition~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq1} does not hold for $A$ and $i_1 = i, i_2 = j, i_3 = k$, then $a_{i\,i}, a_{j\,j}, a_{k\,k}$ are pairwise distinct and consequently
\begin{multline*}
 \begin{vmatrix}
 [2]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right) & [1]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right) & [0]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,j|i,j]\right)\\
  [2]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,k|i,k]\right) & [1]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,k|i,k]\right) & [0]\det \left(A^{(x)}[i,k|i,k]\right)\\
  [2]\det \left(A^{(x)}[j,k|j,k]\right) & [1]\det \left(A^{(x)}[j,k|j,k]\right) & [0]\det \left(A^{(x)}[j,k|j,k]\right)
 \end{vmatrix}\\
=  \begin{vmatrix}
 1 & -a_{i\,i} - a_{j\,j} & a_ia_j\\
  1 & -a_{i\,i} - a_{k\,k} & a_ia_k\\
  1 & -a_{j\,j} - a_{k\,k} & a_ja_k
 \end{vmatrix} = (a_{i\,i} - a_{j\,j})(a_{i\,i} - a_{k\,k})(a_{j\,j}-a_{k\,k}) \neq 0,
\end{multline*}
 which contradicts~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2}.
 
 \subparagraph{$A$ does not satisfy the condition~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq2}} If $1 \le i_1 < i_2 < i_3 < i_4 \le n$ are such that the condition~\eqref{lem:DiagonalR1Crit:eqq2} does not hold for $A$, then assume without loss of generality that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq22203}
a_{i_1\, i_1} \neq a_{i_3\,i_3}, a_{i_3\,i_3}, a_{i_4\,i_4}\quad\mbox{and}\quad a_{i_2\, i_2} \neq a_{i_3\,i_3}, a_{i_4\,i_4}.
\end{equation}
Since $A$ is diagonal, then
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq22201}
 \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|i_1,i_2]\right) = (x - a_{i_1\,i_1})(x - a_{i_2\,i_2}),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq22202}
 \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_3,i_4|i_3,i_4]\right) = (x - a_{i_3\,i_3})(x - a_{i_4\,i_4}).
\end{equation}
Hence,
\begin{multline*}
\operatorname{Res}_{2\,2}\left(\det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|i_1,i_2]\right), \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_3,i_4|i_3,i_4]\right)\right)\\
\overset{\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq22201},\, \eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eq22202}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \operatorname{Res}_{2\,2}\left((x - a_{i_1\,i_1})(x - a_{i_2\,i_2}), (x - a_{i_3\,i_3})(x - a_{i_4\,i_4})\right)\\
\overset{\ref{enum:ResTwoSplit}}{=\joinrel=} \prod_{\substack{1 \le \alpha \le 2\\ 3 \le \beta \le 4}} (x_{i_\alpha\, i_\alpha} - x_{i_\beta\, i_\beta}) \neq 0,
\end{multline*}
 which contradicts~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:R1IndicatorPolyDeg}If $R \in {\mathbb F}[a_{1\,1}, \ldots, a_{n\,n}]$ is a polynomial appearing on the left-hand side of~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1}, \eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12} or~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2}, then $\deg (R) \le 4$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
First, assume that $R \in {\mathbb F}[a_{1\,1}, \ldots, a_{n\,n}]$ is a polynomial appearing on the left-hand side of~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1} or \eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12}. Hence, there are $1 \le i_1 \neq i_2 \le n$, $1 \le j_1 \neq j_2 \le n$,  $1 \le i'_1 \neq i'_2 \le n,$ $1 \le j'_1 \neq j'_2 \le n$ such that
\begin{equation}\notag
R = \operatorname{Res}_{d\, 2}(P, Q),
\end{equation}
where
\[
P = \det\left(A^{(x)}[i_1,i_2|j_1,j_2]\right),\quad Q = \det\left(A^{(x)}[i'_1,i'_2|j'_1,j'_2]\right),\quad d \ge \deg_x\left(P\right)
\]
Let  $\lambda$ be a formal variable. Then
\begin{multline}\label{lem:R1IndicatorPolyDeg:eq2}
R(\lambda A) = \operatorname{Res}_{d\,2}\left(P(\lambda A), Q(\lambda A)\right)\\
= \operatorname{Res}_{d\,2}\left([0]P(\lambda A), \ldots , [d]P(\lambda A); [0]Q(\lambda A),  \ldots, [2]Q(\lambda A)\right)\\
\overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Lemma~\ref{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn}\ref{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn:prop3}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \operatorname{Res}_{d\,2}\left(\lambda^2 [0]P(A), \ldots , \lambda^{2 - d}[d]P(A); \lambda^2 [0]Q(A),  \ldots, [2]Q(A)\right)\\
\overset{\eqref{lem:ResMultOneByScal:eqq1}}{=\joinrel=} \lambda^{2(2-d)}\operatorname{Res}_{d\,2}\left(\lambda^d [0]P(A), \ldots , [d]P(A); \lambda^2 [0]Q( A),  \ldots, [2]Q(A)\right)\\
\overset{\eqref{lem:ResReverseGradHomogen:eqq1}}{=\joinrel=} \lambda^{2(2 - d)}\cdot \lambda^{d \cdot 2}\operatorname{Res}_{d\,2}\left( [0]P(A), \ldots , [d]P(A); [0]Q(A),  \ldots, [2]Q(A)\right)\\
 = \lambda^{4} R(A).
\end{multline}
Therefore, $R$ is a homogeneous polynomial and $\deg(R) \le 4$. 

Second, assume that $R \in {\mathbb F}[a_{1\,1}, \ldots, a_{n\,n}]$ is a polynomial appearing on the left-hand side of~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2}. Hence, there are $1 \le i < j < k \le n$ such that
\begin{equation}\notag
R = \begin{vmatrix}[2]F & [1]F & [0]F\\ [2]G & [1]G & [0]G\\ [2]H & [1]H & [0]H\end{vmatrix},
\end{equation}
where
\[
F = \det\left(A^{(x)}[i, j|i, j]\right),\;\;G = \det\left(A^{(x)}[i, k|i, k]\right),\;\;G = \det\left(A^{(x)}[j, k|j, k]\right),
\]
Let $\lambda$ be a formal variable. Then
\begin{multline*}
R(\lambda A) = \begin{vmatrix}[2]F(\lambda A) & [1]F(\lambda A) & [0]F(\lambda A)\\ [2]G(\lambda A) & [1]G(\lambda A) & [0]G(\lambda A)\\ [2]H(\lambda A) & [1]H(\lambda A) & [0]H(\lambda A)\end{vmatrix}\\
\overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Lemma~\ref{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn}\ref{lem:DegDetAMinusXIn:prop3}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=}  \begin{vmatrix}[2]F(A) & \lambda [1]F(A) & \lambda^2 [0]F(A)\\ [2]G(A) & \lambda [1]G(A) & \lambda^2 [0]G(A)\\ [2]H(A) & \lambda [1]H( A) & \lambda^2 [0]H(A)\end{vmatrix}\\
= \lambda^{1 + 2}\begin{vmatrix}[2]F(A) & [1]F(A) & [0]F(A)\\ [2]G(A) & [1]G(A) &  [0]G(A)\\ [2]H(A) &  [1]H( A) & [0]H(A)\end{vmatrix} = \lambda^3 R(A).\\
\end{multline*}
Therefore, $R$ is a homogeneous polynomial and $\deg(R) \le 3$. Thus, the statement of the lemma holds in all possible cases.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:RNonzeroRAll}Assume that $|{\mathbb F}| > 6$ and $n  \ge 3$. Let $c_1, \ldots, c_m \in {\mathbb F}$ and $B^{(1)}, \ldots, B^{(m)} \in {\mathcal M}_{n\,k}({\mathbb F})$ be such that $(c_1, \ldots, c_m)^t \neq \mathbf 0$. 
If 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eqq1}
\alpha_1 B^{(1)} + \ldots + \alpha_n B^{(m)} \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m \in {\mathbb F}\;\;\mbox{such that}\;\;\sum\limits_{i=1}^{m} c_i\alpha_i\neq 0,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eqq2}
\alpha_1 B^{(1)} + \ldots + \alpha_n B^{(m)} \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})\quad\mbox{for all}\;\;\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m \in {\mathbb F}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of all the polynomials $P \in {\mathbb F}[a_{1\,1}, \ldots, a_{n\,n}]$ appearing on the left-hand side  of~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq1}, \eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq12} or~\eqref{lem:GeneralR1Crit:eqq2}. Lemma~\ref{lem:GeneralR1Crit} means that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq1}
A \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}) \Leftrightarrow \left(\forall P \in \mathcal S \colon P(A) = 0\right)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; A \in {\mathcal M}_n({\mathbb F})
\end{equation}
In addition,
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq2}
\deg(P) \le 4\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; P \in \mathcal S
\end{equation}
by Lemma~\ref{lem:R1IndicatorPolyDeg}.
Let $\mathcal S' \subseteq {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_m]$ be defined by
\begin{equation}
\mathcal S' = \left\{P\left(A\left(x_1,\ldots, x_m\right)\right) | P \in \mathcal S\right\},
\end{equation}
where $A\left(x_1,\ldots, x_m\right) = \left(a_{i\,j}(x_1,\ldots, x_m)\right) \in {\mathcal M}_{n}\left({\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_m]\right)$ is defined by
$$A(x_1,\ldots, x_m) = x_1 B^{(1)} + \ldots + x_m B^{(m)}.$$
From~\eqref{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq1} and~\eqref{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq2} we conclude that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq3}
A\left(x_1,\ldots, x_m\right) \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}) \Leftrightarrow \left(\forall P' \in \mathcal S' \colon P\left(A\left(x_1,\ldots, x_m\right)\right) = 0\right)
\end{equation}
for all $x_1,\ldots, x_m \in {\mathbb F}$ and
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq4}
\deg(P) \overset{\eqref{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq2}}{\le} 4\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; P \in \mathcal S'
\end{equation}
Let $Q = c_1x_1 + \ldots + c_mx_m$. The assumptions of the lemma imply that $Q \neq 0$. In addition,
\begin{equation}\notag
\deg(PQ) \overset{\eqref{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq4}}{\le} 4 + 1 = 5 < |{\mathbb F}|\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; P \in \mathcal S'.
\end{equation}
Hence, 
\[
P'\left(A\left(x_1,\ldots, x_m\right)\right) = 0\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; P' \in \mathcal S',\, x_1, \ldots, x_m \in {\mathbb F}
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:ManyPolyDensityArg} and consequently
\[
\alpha_1 B^{(1)} + \ldots + \alpha_n B^{(m)} = A(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m) \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})\quad\mbox{for all}\;\;\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m \in {\mathbb F}
\]
by~\eqref{lem:RNonzeroRAll:eq3}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lem:RNonzeroRAll} could be considered as an analogue Lemma~2.4 from~\cite{Guterman2025c}, where the set of rank-one rectangular matrices is considered instead of ${\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F}).$
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:RkSum}If $A, B \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$, then $\operatorname{rk}(A + B) \le \operatorname{rk}(A) + \operatorname{rk}(B)$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:SumRankOneEqualScal}Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. If $A^{(1)}, \ldots, A^{(n-1)} \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ are such that  $\operatorname{rk}\left(A^{(i)}\right) \le 1$ for all $1 \le i \le (n-1)$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} A^{(i)}$ is a scalar matrix, then $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} A^{(i)} = 0$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $A = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} A^{(i)}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:RkSum} and the assumptions of the lemma imply that 
$$\operatorname{rk}\left(A\right) = \operatorname{rk}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} A^{(i)}\right) \le  \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{rk}\left( A^{(i)}\right) \le (n-1).$$
Therefore, $A = 0$ because otherwise the assumption that $A$ is a scalar matrix implies that $\operatorname{rk}(A) = n$. This concludes the statement of the lemma.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:OneWayRankOnePlusScalar}Assume that $n \ge 3$. If $A, B \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ and $a, b \in {\mathbb F}$ are such that  $\operatorname{rk}(A), \operatorname{rk}(B) \le 1$ and $A + cI_{n} = B + dI_n,$
then $A = B$ and $c = d.$
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:onedimder}If $f(X) =
a_n x^n + \ldots + a_0 \in {\mathbb F}[x]$, then the \emph{derivative} of $f$ is a polynomial belonging to ${\mathbb F}[x]$ which is denoted by $f'$ and is defined by
\[
f'(X)= na_n x^{n-1} + \ldots + a_1.
\]
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:partDer}
Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$. Then $\frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf v}(\mathbf a) \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n; y_1, \ldots, y_n]$ denotes the \emph{directional derivative of $P$ along $\mathbf v$ at $\mathbf a$} and is defined as a coefficient at $t$ in the following equality in\linebreak ${\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n; y_1, \ldots, y_n; t]$
\[
P(\mathbf a + t \mathbf v) = P(\mathbf a)  + P_1(\mathbf a, \mathbf v)t + \mbox{(terms of higher degree in $t$)},
\]
where the coordinates of $\mathbf a$ correspond to $x_1,\ldots, x_n$, and  the coordinates of $\mathbf v$ correspond to $y_1,\ldots, y_n$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:DirDerLin}
If $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ and $\mathbf a \in {\mathbb F}^n$ are fixed, then the function $\mathbf v \mapsto  \frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf v}(\mathbf a)$ is linear.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:PAV}
Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ and $\mathbf a, \mathbf v \in {\mathbb F}^n$ are fixed. Then by $P_{\mathbf a, \mathbf v} \in {\mathbb F}[t]$ we denote a polynomial defined by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def:PAV}
P_{\mathbf a, \mathbf v} = P(\mathbf a + t \mathbf v).
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:partDer}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ and $\mathbf a, \mathbf v \in {\mathbb F}^n$. Then $\deg(P_{\mathbf a, \mathbf v}) \le \deg(P)$ and 
\begin{equation}\label{def:partDer:eqq1}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf v}(\mathbf a) = P'_{\mathbf a, \mathbf v}(0)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; \mathbf v \in {\mathbb F}^n.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:PLFunc} Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ and $\mathbf a \in {\mathbb F}^n$. By $l_{P,\mathbf a} \colon \mathbb F^n \to \mathbb F$ we denote a linear function defined by
\[
l_{P, \mathbf a}(\mathbf v) = \frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf v}(\mathbf a)\qquad(\mathbf v \in {\mathbb F}^n).
\]
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:LP}
Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$. By $\mathcal L_P \subseteq ({\mathbb F}^n)^*$ we denote the vector space spanned by all the linear functions of the form $l_{P, \mathbf a}$ for some $\mathbf a \in {\mathbb F}^n.$ That is,
\[
\mathcal L_P = \operatorname{span} (\{\mathbf v \mapsto \frac{\partial P}{\partial \mathbf v}(\mathbf a) \mid \mathbf a \in \mathbb F^n\}).
\]
Equivalently, $\mathcal L_{P} \subseteq {{\mathbb F}^n}^*$ spanned by the range of the gradient field of $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{thm:surjpres}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ be a polynomial such that $\deg (P) < |{\mathbb F}|$. If  $\phi, \psi \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^n$ are such that
\begin{equation*}
P(\mathbf{x} + \lambda \mathbf{y}) = P(\phi(\mathbf{x}) + \lambda \psi(\mathbf{y}))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb {\mathbb F}^n,\; \lambda \in {\mathbb F},
\end{equation*}
and $\phi$ is surjective, then $l \circ \psi \in \mathcal L_P$ for all $l \in \mathcal L_P.$
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:SurjPresComp}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ be a polynomial such that $\deg (P) < |{\mathbb F}|$. If  $\phi, \psi \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^n$ are such that
\begin{equation*}
P(\mathbf{x} + \lambda \mathbf{y}) = P(\phi(\mathbf{x}) + \lambda \psi(\mathbf{y}))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb {\mathbb F}^n,\; \lambda \in {\mathbb F},
\end{equation*}
and $\phi$ is surjective, then $\psi(\mathbf v) \in \left({\mathcal L}_P\right)^0$ for all $\mathbf v \in \left({\mathcal L}_P\right)^0$.
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lem:eqpqd}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n], Q \in {\mathbb F}[x_1, \ldots, x_m]$, $\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1\in {\mathbb F}^n$ and $\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2 \in {\mathbb F}^m$. If $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$ and
\begin{equation}\label{lem:eqpqd:eqlem1}
P(\mathbf x_1 + \lambda \mathbf y_1) = Q(\mathbf x_2 + \lambda \mathbf y_2)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\lambda \in {\mathbb F}, 
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation*}\label{lem:eqpqd:eqlem2}
l_{P,\mathbf x_1}(\mathbf y_1) = l_{Q, \mathbf x_2}(\mathbf y_2).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Indeed, the equality~\eqref{lem:eqpqd:eqlem1} implies that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:eqpqd:eq1}
P_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1}(\lambda) = Q_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2}(\lambda)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\lambda \in {\mathbb F},
\end{equation}
where $P_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1}, Q_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2} \in {\mathbb F}[t]$ are defined in Definition~\ref{def:PAV}. Since $\deg(P_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1}) \leq \deg(P)$ and $\deg(Q_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2}) \leq \deg(Q)$ by Lemma~\ref{def:partDer}, and $\deg(P) < |{\mathbb F}|$ by the statement of the lemma, then $\deg(P_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1}) < |{\mathbb F}|$ and $\deg(Q_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2}) < |{\mathbb F}|$. Therefore, from~\eqref{lem:eqpqd:eq1} and Lemma~\ref{DegFGLessEqual} we conclude that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:eqpd:eq2}
P_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1} = Q_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2}\;\;\mbox{as elements of}\;{\mathbb F}[t].
\end{equation}
Hence, $P'_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1} = Q'_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2}$ and, in particular,
$P'_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1}(0) = Q'_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2}(0)$

Therefore,
\[
l_{P,\mathbf x_1}(\mathbf y_1) = P'_{\mathbf x_1, \mathbf y_1}(0) = Q'_{\mathbf x_2, \mathbf y_2}(0) =  l_{Q, \mathbf x_2}(\mathbf y_2)
\]
by Lemma~\ref{def:partDer} and the definitions of $l_{P,\mathbf x_1}$ and $l_{Q,\mathbf x_2}$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lem:DimLPUnderLinConvInj}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n], Q \in {\mathbb F}[x_1, \ldots, x_m]$ be such that\linebreak  $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$. If there is a injective linear map $T \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^m$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eqq1}
P(\mathbf x) = Q(T(\mathbf x))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^{n},
\end{equation}
 then $\dim(\mathcal L_P) \le \dim(\mathcal L_Q).$
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By contradiction. Suppose that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq2}
d = \dim(\mathcal L_P) > \dim(\mathcal L_Q).
\end{equation} Let $\mathbf x_1, \ldots, \mathbf x_d \in {\mathbb F}^n$ be such that the functionals $l_{P, \mathbf x_1}, \ldots l_{P, \mathbf x_d}$ form a basis of $\mathcal L_P$. This implies that 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq1}
l_{P, \mathbf x_1}, \ldots l_{P, \mathbf x_d}\;\;\mbox{are linearly independent}.
\end{equation}
From the inequality~\eqref{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq2} we obtain that there is $c_1, \ldots, c_d \in {\mathbb F}$ such that $(c_1,\ldots, c_d)^t \neq \mathbf 0$ and
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq4}
\sum_{i=1}^d c_i  l_{Q, T(\mathbf x_i)} = 0 
\end{equation}

The equality~\eqref{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eqq1} implies that
\begin{equation*}
P(\mathbf x_i + \lambda \mathbf y) = Q(T(\mathbf x_i) + \lambda T(\mathbf y))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le d, \; \mathbf y \in {\mathbb F}^n, \;\lambda \in {\mathbb F}.
\end{equation*}
Hence,
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq3}
l_{P,\mathbf x_i}(\mathbf y) = l_{Q, T(\mathbf x_i)}(T(\mathbf  y))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le d, \; \mathbf y \in {\mathbb F}^n
\end{equation}
by Lemma~\ref{lem:eqpqd}. Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{i=1}^d c_i  l_{Q, T(\mathbf x_i)}(T(\mathbf y)) \overset{\eqref{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq3}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \sum_{i=1}^d c_i  l_{P, \mathbf x_i}(\mathbf y) \overset{\eqref{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq4}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} 0 \;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;  \mathbf y \in {\mathbb F}^n
\end{equation*}
which contradicts with~\eqref{lem:DimLPUnderLinConv:eq1}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:DimLPUnderLinConvBij}
Let $P, Q \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ be such that $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$. If there is a bijective linear map $T \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^n$ such that $P(\mathbf x) = Q(T(\mathbf x))$ for all $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^{n}$, then $\dim(\mathcal L_P) = \dim(\mathcal L_Q).$
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:PolyPointInv}
Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ and $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n$ is fixed. Then by $P_{(\mathbf x)} \in {\mathbb F}[a_1,\ldots, a_n, \lambda]$ we denote a polynomial defined by
\[
P_{(\mathbf x)}(\mathbf a, \lambda) = P(\mathbf a + \lambda \mathbf x)
\] 
and by $P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(0)}, \ldots, P_{(\mathbf x)}^{\left(\deg_\lambda\left(P^{(\mathbf x)}\right)\right)} \in {\mathbb F}[a_1,\ldots, a_n]$ we denote coefficients of $\lambda$ in the expansion
\[
P_{(\mathbf x)}(\mathbf a, \lambda) = P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(0)}(\mathbf a) + \lambda P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(1)}(\mathbf a) + \ldots + \lambda^{\deg_\lambda \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right)} P_{(\mathbf x)}^{\left(\deg_\lambda\left(P^{(\mathbf x)}\right)\right)}(\mathbf a)
\]
of $P^{(\mathbf x)}$ by the powers of $\lambda$ (in the expansion above $P_{(\mathbf x)}$ is considered as an element of ${\mathbb F}[a_1,\ldots, a_n, \lambda]$).
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lem:DegsPPart}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ and $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n$ is fixed. Then 
\[\deg \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}\right) \le \deg_\lambda  \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) \le \deg (P)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda  \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Indeed,
\begin{multline*}
\deg \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}\right) \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize By the definition of $P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}$}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \deg \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) - i\\
 \le \deg_\lambda  \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right)  \le \deg (P^{(\mathbf x)}) \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize By the definition of $P_{(\mathbf x)}$}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \deg (P)
\end{multline*}
for all $1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda  \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right).$
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq}
Let $P, P' \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n],$  $\mathbf x, \mathbf x' \in {\mathbb F}^n$ be such that\linebreak $\deg(P), \deg(P') < |{\mathbb F}|$ and $P_{(\mathbf x)}(\mathbf a, \lambda) = {P'}_{(\mathbf x')}(\mathbf a, \lambda)$ for all $\mathbf a \in {\mathbb F}^n, \lambda \in {\mathbb F}$. Then 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq:eqq11}
\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) = \deg_\lambda\left(P'_{(\mathbf x')}\right)
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq:eqq1}
P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}=  {P'}_{(\mathbf x')}^{(i)}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right). 
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
From Lemma~\ref{lem:DegsPPart} and the assumptions of the lemma we conclude that
\begin{equation*}
\deg_\lambda \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) < |{\mathbb F}|\;\;\mbox{and}\;\; \deg_{\lambda}\left(P'_{(\mathbf x')}\right) < |{\mathbb F}|.
\end{equation*}
This allows us to apply the Corollary~\ref{DegFGLessEqual} to $P_{(\mathbf x)}$ and $P'_{(\mathbf x')}$ and infer that $P_{(\mathbf x)}$ and $P'_{(\mathbf x')}$ are equal as elements of ${\mathbb F}[a_1,\ldots, a_n, \lambda]$. Therefore, their corresponding coefficients are equal to each other. Hence, the equalities~\eqref{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq:eqq11} and~\eqref{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq:eqq1} hold.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n]$ be such that $\deg(P)< |{\mathbb F}|$, and $\mathbf y, \mathbf y'$ be such that $\mathbf y = \mathbf y' \pmod{\operatorname{rad}(P)}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq1111}
\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y)}\right) = \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y')}\right)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq1112}
\dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}}\right) = \dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf y')}^{(i)}}\right)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y)}\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $\mathbf z = \mathbf y - \mathbf y'$ and $P' \in {\mathbb F}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ be defined by $P(\mathbf x) = P(\mathbf x + \mathbf z)$. This definition implies that $\deg(P') = \deg(P)$. On the one hand,
\begin{equation*}
P' = P
\end{equation*}
because $\mathbf z \in \operatorname{rad}(P)$ and $\deg(P)< |{\mathbb F}|$. Hence,
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eq1}
P_{(\mathbf y')} = {P'}_{(\mathbf y')}\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;P_{(\mathbf y')}^{(i)} = {P'}_{(\mathbf y')}^{(i)}\qquad\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y)}\right).
\end{equation}
On the other hand,
\begin{multline*}
{P'}_{(\mathbf y')}(\mathbf a, \lambda) = {P'}(\mathbf a + \lambda \mathbf y') = P(\mathbf a + \mathbf z + \lambda \mathbf y')\\
= P(\mathbf a + \mathbf z + \lambda (\mathbf y - \mathbf z)) = P(\mathbf a + \lambda \mathbf y + (1 - \lambda) \mathbf z)\\
\overset{\scriptsize \mathbf z \in \operatorname{rad}(P)}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} P(\mathbf a + \lambda \mathbf y) = {P}_{(\mathbf y)}(\mathbf a, \lambda).
\end{multline*}
By applying Lemma~\ref{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq} to $P, \mathbf y$ and $P', \mathbf y'$, correspondingly, we obtain that
 \begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq11}
\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y)}\right) = \deg_\lambda\left(P'_{(\mathbf y')}\right)
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq1}
P_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}=  {P'}_{(\mathbf y')}^{(i)}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y)}\right). 
\end{equation}
Finally, by combining~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq11} and~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq1} with~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eq1} we obtain~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq1111} and~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariantForRad:eqq1112}, respectively.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
\label{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n],$ $Q \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_m],$ $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n,$ $\mathbf y \in {\mathbb F}^m,$ $T \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^m$ be such that $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$, $T$ is a linear map sending $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$ and satisfying 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eqq1}
P(\mathbf z) = Q(T(\mathbf z))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf z \in {\mathbb F}^n.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eqq2}
P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}(\mathbf z) =  Q_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}(T(\mathbf z))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf z \in {\mathbb F}^n,\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right). 
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Since the map $T$ is linear, then the composition $Q' = Q \circ T$ is a polynomial (i.e., element of ${\mathbb F}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$) and $\deg (Q') \le \deg (Q)$. Together with the initial assumption that $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$ and the equality~\eqref{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eqq1} this allows us to apply Lemma~\ref{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq} to $P$ and $P'$ and obtain that
\begin{equation}\label{TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eq1}
P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}=  {Q'}_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right). 
\end{equation}
In addition, the equality  $Q' = Q \circ T$ infers the equalities 
\begin{equation}\label{TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eq2}
{Q'}_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)} = {Q}_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)} \circ T\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(Q_{(\mathbf x)}\right).
\end{equation} 
Then, by substituting~\eqref{TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eq2} in~\eqref{TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eq1} and evaluating it in $\mathbf z \in {\mathbb F}^n$, we obtain~\eqref{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eqq2}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
\label{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n],$ $Q \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_m],$ $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n,$ $\mathbf y \in {\mathbb F}^m,$ $T \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^m$ be such that $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$, $T$ is a linear map sending $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$ and satisfying 
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eqq1}
P(\mathbf z) = Q(T(\mathbf z))\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf z \in {\mathbb F}^n.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eqq2}
\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) \leq \deg_\lambda\left(Q_{(\mathbf y)}\right)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eqq3}
\dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}}\right) \leq \dim\left(\mathcal L_{Q_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}}\right)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Note that by applying Lemma~\ref{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI} to $P, Q, \mathbf x, \mathbf y$ and $T$ we obtain that the equality~\eqref{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eqq2} holds.

Let us prove the inequality~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eqq2}. For this let $j \ge \deg_\lambda\left(Q_{(\mathbf y)}\right)$ be nonnegative integer. Then $Q_{(\mathbf y)}^{(j)} = 0$ and consequently
\begin{equation*}
P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(j)}(\mathbf a) \overset{\eqref{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eqq2}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} Q_{(\mathbf y)}^{(j)}(T(\mathbf a)) = 0\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;\mathbf a \in {\mathbb F}^n.
\end{equation*}
Hence, $P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(j)} = 0$ by Corollary~\ref{DegFLessZero}. Therefore, $\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) \le \deg_\lambda\left(Q_{(\mathbf y)}\right)$ as required.

In order to prove the inequality~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eqq3}, note Lemma~\eqref{lem:DegsPPart} together with the assumption $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$ implies that
\begin{equation}\label{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eq3}
\deg \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}\right) < |{\mathbb F}|\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\deg \left(Q_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}\right)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\;1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda  \left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) 
\end{equation}

Relying on the equality~\eqref{lem:TPreservesPThenTPreservesPI:eqq2} and the inequalities in~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eq3}, we apply\linebreak Lemma~\ref{lem:DimLPUnderLinConvInj} to $P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}$, $Q_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}$ and $T$ for every $1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right)$ and obtain the inequality~\eqref{lem:DegAndLPAreInvariant:eqq3}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-16: body_md -->
\label{cor:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariant}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n],$ $Q \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_m],$ $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n,$ $\mathbf y \in {\mathbb F}^m,$ $T \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^m$ be such that $\deg(P), \deg(Q) < |{\mathbb F}|$, $T$ is a bijective linear map sending $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$ and satisfying $P(\mathbf z) = Q(T(\mathbf z))$ for all $\mathbf z \in {\mathbb F}^n$.  Then
\[
\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) = \deg_\lambda\left(Q_{(\mathbf y)}\right)
\]
and
\[
\dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}}\right) = \dim\left(\mathcal L_{Q_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}}\right)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right).
\]
<!-- end corollary-16 -->
<!-- lemma-36: body_md -->
\label{lem:DegAndPartPreservance}Let $P \in {\mathbb F}[x_1,\ldots, x_n],$ $\mathbf x \in {\mathbb F}^n,$ $\mathbf y \in {\mathbb F}^n,$ $T \colon {\mathbb F}^n \to {\mathbb F}^n$ be such that $\deg(P) < |{\mathbb F}|$, $T$ is a bijective linear map such that 
\[
T(\mathbf x) = \mathbf y \pmod{\operatorname{rad}(P)}
\] and $P(\mathbf z) = P(T(\mathbf z))$ for all $\mathbf z \in {\mathbb F}^n$.  Then
\[
\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) = \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y)}\right)
\]
and
\[
\dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}}\right) = \dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}}\right)\;\;\mbox{for all}\;\; 1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-36 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Indeed, if $\mathbf y' = T(\mathbf x)$, then
\[
\deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right) \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Corollary~\ref{cor:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariant}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x')}\right) \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Lemma~\ref{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=}  \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf y)}\right)
\]
and
\[
\dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf x)}^{(i)}}\right) \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Corollary~\ref{cor:DegAndLPAreReallyInvariant}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf x')}^{(i)}}\right) \overset{\mbox{\scriptsize Lemma~\ref{lem:IfPolyEqThenCompEq}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \dim\left(\mathcal L_{P_{(\mathbf y)}^{(i)}}\right)
\]
for all $1 \le i \le \deg_\lambda\left(P_{(\mathbf x)}\right).$
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-37: body_md -->
\label{lem:SimPlusScalSameInvD} Assume that $n \ge 2$ and $|{\mathbb F}| > n(n-1)$. Let $X, Y \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be such that $X$ is similar to $Y + cI_n$ for some $c \in {\mathbb F}$. Then $\deg_\lambda (\operatorname{D}_{(X)}) = \deg_\lambda (\operatorname{D}_{(Y)})$ and $\dim\left(\mathcal L_{\operatorname{D}_{(X)}^{(i)}}\right) = \dim\left(\mathcal L_{\operatorname{D}_{(Y)}^{(i)}}\right)$ for all $1 \le \deg_\lambda (\operatorname{D}_{(X)}).$
<!-- end lemma-37 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let $T \colon {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F}) \to {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be a linear map corresponding to a similarity transformation sending $X$ to $Y + cI_n$. This map is bijective as a similarity and preserves $\operatorname{D}$ by the property~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyS} of the matrix discriminant. In addition, $Y + cI_n = Y \pmod{\operatorname{rad}(\operatorname{D})}$ because $cI_n \in \operatorname{rad}(\operatorname{D})$ by the property~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyC} of the matrix discriminant. From this we conclude that the required equalities hold by Lemma~\ref{lem:DegAndPartPreservance} applied to $X, Y, \operatorname{D}$ and $T$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-38: body_md -->
\label{lem:SimPlusScalSameInvD2} Assume that $n \ge 2$ and $|{\mathbb F}| > \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ and $\operatorname{char}({\mathbb F}) = 2$. Let $X, Y \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$ be such that $Y$ is similar to $X + cI_n$ for some $c \in {\mathbb F}$. Then $\deg_\lambda \left(\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}_{(X)}\right) = \deg_\lambda \left(\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}_{(Y)}\right)$ and $\dim\left(\mathcal L_{\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}_{(X)}^{(i)}}\right) = \dim\left(\mathcal L_{\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}_{(Y)}^{(i)}}\right)$ for all $1 \le \deg_\lambda \left(\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}_{(X)}\right).$
<!-- end lemma-38 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The proof of this lemma is similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:SimPlusScalSameInvD}. We only apply  the property~\ref{enum:D2PropertyS} of $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}$ instead of the property~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyS} of the matrix discriminant and the property~\ref{enum:D2PropertyC} of $\operatorname{{\mathfrak B}}$ instead of the property~\ref{enum:DiscPropertyC} of the matrix discriminant.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-39: body_md -->
\label{lem:RankOneScalImpliesLowDeg}Assume that $n \ge 1$ and $|{\mathbb F}| > n(n-1)$. Let $X \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$. If $X \in {\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})$,

then
\begin{equation}\label{lem:RankOneScalImpliesLowDeg:eqq1}
\deg_{\lambda} \left(\operatorname{D}_{(X)}\right) \le 2n - 2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-39 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We will prove sequentially that the statement of the lemma holds in the following cases
\begin{enumerate}[label=Case (\alph*), ref=(\alph*), leftmargin=*]
\item\label{lem:RankOneScalImpliesLowDeg:part1} $X = (r E_{1\,1} + s E_{1\,2})$, where $r, s \in {\mathbb F}$;
\item\label{lem:RankOneScalImpliesLowDeg:part3} $X$ is an arbitrary element of ${\mathfrak R}_n({\mathbb F})$.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Case~\ref{lem:RankOneScalImpliesLowDeg:part1}} Assume that $X = (r E_{1\,1} + s E_{1\,2})$, where $s, t \in {\mathbb F}$. Let $A \in {\mathcal M}_{n}({\mathbb F})$. Consider $p_{A + \lambda X}(t)$:
\[
p_{A + \lambda X}(t) = \left|
\begin{matrix}
t -  a_{1\,1} - \lambda r  & - a_{1\,2} - \lambda s & \ldots & - a_{1\,n} \\
- a_{2\,1}     & t -  a_{2\,2}        & \ldots &  - a_{2\,n} \\
\vdots          & \vdots                & \ddots & \vdots\\
- a_{n\,1}     & -  a_{n\,2}        & \ldots & t - a_{n\,n}
\end{matrix}
\right| \in {\mathbb F}[\lambda, t; a_{1\,1}, \ldots, a_{n\,n}].
\]
Expanding this determinant along the first row we obtain that
\[
p_{A + \lambda X}(t) = P + (k\lambda  + l)Q
\]
